169.context: Fernando's drink wager leads to a discussion of observation, a couple's actual breakup and a recruitment offer decided by coin toss. Keep the game rules, alternating win/loss and repeat-visit branches, the evidence for his inference, his confidence and the lucky/unlucky outcomes distinct.
notes: The wager is a drink, not an invented coin fee. Players take one to three coins; the person taking the last loses.
The couple is breaking up, not demonstrably married or divorcing.
His claimed luck is characterization, not narrator proof of supernatural power.
meanings: In a returning-visitor variant, he insists that coming here means accepting the challenge.
Greets a new face and proposes a simple game with a drink as the stake.
Explains that each player takes a chosen number from one to three coins on each turn.
The player taking the last coin loses; he considers the rules simple and starts.
In his winning branch, he claims the drink.
Enjoys it, thanks the visitor and says goodbye.
In his losing branch, he admits a rare defeat and offers what he owes.
Hodram declines the drink for now and asks about his confidence in gambling.
He says observation and luck are what matter in gambling.
Claims to possess both and to have been born for gambling.
Hodram doubts that he is perceptive.
He warns against judging by appearances.
Points out a couple whose words he cannot hear and asks what Hodram thinks they are discussing.
Hodram assumes the man is courting her.
Fernando considers this elementary: they are discussing a breakup.
Hodram reacts questioningly.
Fernando tells him to watch.
The woman says she can no longer accept the man's thinking and accuses him of selfishness.
The man says she may think as she likes, but he considers her selfish too.
She concludes that they should stop seeing each other.
He agrees that if both feel this way, this is the end of their relationship.
Hodram silently witnesses this.
Fernando points out that his prediction was right.
Hodram is impressed and asks how he knew.
The woman clenched a fist beneath the table, suppressing anger rather than discussing love.
The man never looked at her; Fernando questions whether he seemed to be facing a woman he loved.
Hodram acknowledges the excellent perception.
Fernando says such insight lets him read an opponent's intentions or next play.
His exceptional luck does the rest, allowing him to win.
Hodram thinks the talent is wasted on gambling alone and invites him aboard.
Fernando is surprised by the sudden proposal.
He has time to spare; he will toss a coin and come along if it lands heads.
In another approach, Hodram again declines a drink and directly asks him aboard.
Fernando recognizes the repeated request and will consult the coin again.
On rejection, he refuses to entrust his life to an unlucky man and bids farewell.
On acceptance, he declares the matter decided and will stake his life on Hodram.
Introduces himself as Fernando Dias and credits luck for the meeting or outcome.
Hodram says he is counting on Fernando's abilities.
In a separate reaction, Fernando grumbles that things have been lean or unpromising lately.

170.context: Julio noisily condemns bad drink, demands something better and maneuvers himself aboard regardless of the advice question or the denial of carrying good alcohol. Preserve his pushiness, self-styled experience, Hodram's restrained tolerance and Gerhard's interrupted objection. The two recruitment routes are alternatives, not consecutive arrivals.
notes: Old-man address does not establish kinship; preserve Julio, not Grandpa.
The source says alcohol generally; do not narrow it to a named wine or spirit without item/condition support.
Call me a veteran or old hand describes experience, not an invented military service record.
His intuition and accusation of lying are his assertions; do not treat them as independently proved narrator facts.
meanings: An older man loudly declares that something is unacceptable.
Hodram reacts questioningly.
The man repeats the complaint with increasingly emphatic volume.
Hodram privately assumes he is a drunk.
The man calls sharply to them.
Hodram remains silent.
The man complains that young people nowadays are hopeless.
Hodram privately recognizes the familiar older-person complaint.
The man condemns them for drinking such terrible alcohol.
Hodram privately feels trapped or exasperated.
The man asks why he looks dissatisfied.
Hodram suggests that if he dislikes the drink, he need not drink it.
The man argues that wanting a drink leaves him little choice, citing the idea of necessity overriding preference.
Gerhard pointedly suggests drinking quietly and considering the people nearby.
The man begins explaining that even if necessity makes him drink bad alcohol and complain...
What he really wants is good alcohol; he asks Hodram to provide some.
Promises that he may behave quietly if given something good.
Hodram privately sighs at the situation.
The man demands it quickly and claims intuition tells him Hodram must have a fine drink.
In the affirmative branch, he is impressed that Hodram knows good drink.
Hodram disclaims expert tasting knowledge but understands ordinary trade value.
The man is interested in trade and claims some knowledge of it himself.
Hodram asks whether he traded aboard ships.
The man confirms it and asks to be called a veteran or experienced hand.
Hodram asks permission to put a question to him.
The man asks what he wants to know.
For a straightforward question, he approves the receptive attitude and desire to learn.
Proposes setting off and asks where their ship is.
For a question intended as a test, he realizes the intention and refuses to be easily tested.
Insists that a contrary person needs firm instruction, beginning with recognizing good alcohol.
Demands that they stop staring and show him aboard.
Hodram is taken aback.
The man assumes they will take him along: he has too much to teach for one or two days.
Hodram pauses.
Introduces himself as Julio Erneco and asks for a good association.
Hodram somewhat hesitantly reciprocates.
Gerhard objects that the admiral has not actually granted permission to board.
Hodram allows it anyway.
Julio looks forward excitedly to being at sea again after a while away.
In the denial branch, he accuses Hodram of lying or feigning ignorance because he is old and demands the truth.
Hodram backtracks that he was just about to look for good drink during their voyage.
Julio enthusiastically seizes on the voyage and decides to accompany them.
Hodram is startled.
Julio laughs at the surprise: appearances aside, he is still an active seaman.
Despite his age, he expects to be quite useful.
Gerhard again objects that the admiral has not approved boarding.
Hodram again accepts the situation.
In this alternative introduction, Julio Erneco asks to be treated well from now on.
